Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

Overall, I found this an exciting and engaging story. It places a classic nodulation defective mutant into a plausible protein complex and provides solid support for its cellular role in maintaining the infection thread through high-quality imaging and phenotypic analysis. This work established a hierarchy of "infectosome" assembly using genetics and localization of components. I have no major experimental or data analysis concerns. In general, the figures are well laid out and the images are of excellent quality, so the data are easy to evaluate. The sample sizes and statistical measurements are appropriate for the conclusions the authors draw.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

I enjoyed reading this meticulous work. It is very informative and the findings will be highly relevant to the field. However, I also have a number of puzzling observations. I raise them here in the order they appear:

1. In Figure 3A, panels on the right half show the localization inside the infection thread. However, the close-up (in particular panel 2 and 3) does not exactly match the dotted area in panel 1. Several GFP dots, representing bacteria, are missing in the close up. Did the authors happen to use different optical sections for the lower- and high-magnification images?

2. On Line 199 the authors stated that "IT tip-associated puncta encased the growing IT tip". However in Figure 3-supplement 1A the RPG punctum does not look like a case of any sort. This seems an unnecessary overstatement.

3. In Figure 3-supplement 3D, why does the mCherry channel appear to be white even in the merged panel? This makes it hard to assess the claim that RPG-NT is mainly in the nucleus.

4. In the GFP panel of Figure 3B, how did the authors differentiate the signal of VPY-GFP from that of 3xNowGFP? I assume the latter is used as a transformation marker. Does the confocal settings avoid or exclude fluorescence from NowGFP? This is important, as it seems to be the basis for concluding that VPY-GFP "was also diffusely visible in the cytoplasm".

5. The co-IP signals are rather weak for the interacting partner. Most often, co-IP results are validated both ways (not only A IPs B, but B also IPs A). Are the proteins expressed well? If they are, I wonder why the authors isolated protoplasts, rather than directly extracting proteins from whole leaves. Surely most samples are lost during protoplasting.

6. The rpg mutant does form elongating infection threads, albeit highly irregular ones. Yet in Figures 3E, 5A, and 5B, one cannot see the file of bacteria along the mutant root hair. The structure shown here in the rpg mutant is more akin to infection chambers. In 4A, the mutant seems to be just starting an infection thread. Why did the authors not choose elongating infection threads like they did in Figures 1B and 2B?

7. The distinct puncta of VPY disappears in the rpg mutant (Figure 3-supplement 5). Can the authors tell whether the cause is diffuse localization, reduced total protein levels, or reduced transcription in the absence of RPG?

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

1. The authors report larger infection threads in rpg mutants than in WT. Could the morphology of uninfected root hair in rpg mutant explain this phenotype? Quantification of the diameter of noninfected RH in WT and rpg mutants should allow the authors to rule out this hypothesis. Moreover, the author reported that TEM micrographs of nodule infected cells revealed "larger IT structures present in nodule tissues of rpg-1 compared to WT but WT-like cell organization and symbiosome morphology": quantification is needed here.

2. To gain more insights into the structural requirements for RPG functionality, the authors generated a series of truncation derivatives and tested them for their capability to genetically complement rpg-1. They showed that the major molecular determinant conferring functionality to RPG resides in its coiled-coil domain. It is not clearly stated how the authors check that the constructs were expressed? It is particularly important for two variants that do not complement the rpg mutant. The authors should explain how they assessed that the constructs were stable and therefore the phenotype observed is not due to an absence of the truncated version but rather to a loss in its activity. It will be appreciated to have the number of independent transformants in the legend of the figure or in the panels (rather than in the material and method).

3. The authors clearly showed that RPG protein has a punctate localization. mCherry-RPG clearly co-localized with VPY-GFP in punctate structures located at the tip of the infection threads and in the cytoplasm connecting the nucleus to the infection threads tip of infected root hairs. However, quantifications are missing for all the data presented in Figure 3A-C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-D, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A-D.

4. The author showed that RPG co-purified with EXO70H4 and VPY indicating that these proteins indeed belong to the same complex. Moreover, they showed that the major molecular determinant conferring functionality to RPG resides in its coiled-coil domain. Does the CC domain important for RPG interaction with VAPYRIN (VPY)/mCherry-EXO70H4? Furthermore, there is no clear indication of the number of times this experiment has been replicated.

While no quantification is presented, the authors showed with clear illustrations that the mCherry-RPG-NT construct which does not complement the rpg mutant remained diffuse in the cytoplasm and preferentially accumulated in the nucleus of transformed root hairs. It would be interesting to repeat this analysis (mCherry-RPG-CC, mCherry-RPG-tCC, mCherry-RPG-NT) in WT plants: These complementary analyses will allow the authors to further evaluate if the function of RPG depends on its localization or on its interaction with protein partners.

6. In Figure 4, they reported that in uninfected growing root hairs, PI(4,5)P2 was enriched at the apical membrane domain while at the onset of infection PI(4,5)P2 was locally and specifically enriched at the membrane surrounding invading bacteria emerging from the infection chamber. The observations presented in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 5 should be quantified. Did the authors try to over-express RPG and check for a potential increase in membrane polarity? How do these increases in PIP2 polarity occur? Is it via the transcriptional regulation of the PIP2 metabolism or via the trafficking/activity of the PIP2 regulating enzymes? Some pieces of information should be added at least in the discussion of the paper.

7. They further observed that local PI(4,5)P2 enrichment also occurred on the basal membrane of root hairs hosting polarized infection threads and on the apical membrane of underlying cortical neighboring cells. It is not clear to me how the authors know that this membrane belongs to the infected cell and is not part of another cell that is about to initiate a root hair. Imaging in 3D will help to understand the topology here.

8. Since nuclear movement appeared uncoupled from the infection threads' growth in rpg, the authors tested the implication of the MTs in this phenomenon. Even if the authors are citing other studies showing the role of MTs, it is not clear to me why the actin cytoskeleton was excluded from this analysis. Maybe the authors should consider discussing it, in particular since the actin cytoskeleton is important for polar growth and might be linked to PIP2 polarity.

9. By comparing microtubule organization in WT and rpg root hairs harboring the infection threads using live-cell imaging, they reported the loss of nuclear-mediated IT guidance occurs in rpg "in the majority of the case", "often". Please quantify more deeply the results obtained in Figure 5A (in particular in the corresponding text of the result section). Why the nucleus is not visible in magenta in the right panels?

10. Regarding the polar secretion of NPL which requires functional RPG, is there a direct role of the membrane polarization (or PIP2) in the exocytosis of cell wall modifying enzyme NODULE PECTATE LYASE (NPL)? Maybe some information could be added in the discussion of the manuscript about the general knowledge from the literature.

11. The authors should consider adding a model for the different molecular components they studied in the context of this biotic interaction.

claims.evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings and cites Gage, 2004 and Yamazaki and Hayashi, 2015.

results.result: Two independent rpg mutant alleles (rpg-1 in A17 and rpg-2 in R108) exhibit enlarged, bulbous infection threads with significantly increased and variable diameter compared to wild-type, while root hair diameter remains normal. Both mutants show reduced nodulation and poorly colonized nodules, but normal symbiosome morphology, confirming RPG is essential for IT development but not bacterial release or nodule organogenesis.
results.evaluation: The phenotypic characterization is comprehensive with two independent alleles, quantitative measurements (C5, C16), appropriate controls (C7), and multiple imaging modalities (confocal, TEM). Statistical significance is demonstrated (C5, C11, C16), and the specificity of the IT defect is established by normal root hair diameter (C7) and symbiosome morphology (C15, C17). The genetic confirmation with independent alleles in different backgrounds strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Structure-function analysis reveals that RPG's coiled-coil domain (aa 331-1255) is necessary and sufficient for IT complementation, though with reduced efficiency compared to full-length protein. The N-terminal 143 amino acids of the coiled-coil are critical for function, while the N-terminal region (NLS, NT-C2, IDR) contributes to full functionality but is not sufficient alone.
results.evaluation: The complementation assays systematically test deletion constructs (C21-C25) with quantitative phenotypic scoring (Figure 2C). The results clearly demonstrate that RPG-CC rescues the phenotype while RPG-tCC and RPG-NT do not (C22, C23, C25), supporting the functional importance of the coiled-coil domain (C24). The lower efficiency of RPG-CC versus RPG-FL (C26) indicates the N-terminal region contributes to optimal function. However, C27 is speculative about the regulatory mechanism.

results.result: RPG localizes to discrete cytoplasmic puncta in root hairs following rhizobial inoculation, with puncta positioned near the root hair tip in uninfected cells, adjacent to the infection chamber in curled root hairs, and at both the IT tip and perinuclear region in infected root hairs. This localization pattern differs from the exclusively nuclear localization previously reported in heterologous N. benthamiana expression.
results.evaluation: The localization data are based on systematic live-cell imaging with quantified frequencies of observation (C28-C33). FLIM is used to distinguish RPG signal from autofluorescence and nuclear markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D, C34). The heterologous expression in N. benthamiana confirms punctate localization also occurs in this system (C37-C39), validating the observation. The contrast with prior work (C36) is appropriately noted.

results.result: The coiled-coil domain is necessary and sufficient for RPG localization to cytoplasmic puncta, with deletion of aa 331-473 abolishing function but not localization. The N-terminal region enhances targeting/accumulation to IT tips, as RPG-CC shows reduced IT tip localization (7/22) compared to RPG-FL (17/21) despite consistent perinuclear puncta labeling.
results.evaluation: The localization analysis of deletion constructs (C40-C41) is systematic and quantified. The observation that RPG-tCC and RPG-CC both localize to puncta while only RPG-CC is functional (C40-C41) separates localization from function. The reduced IT tip accumulation of RPG-CC (C43) correlates with its reduced complementation efficiency (C26), providing internal consistency. The inference about N-terminal contribution to targeting (C42-C43) is well-supported by the comparative data.

results.result: RPG co-localizes with VPY and LIN in IT tip- and perinuclear-associated puncta (infectosome foci). Co-immunoprecipitation demonstrates RPG interacts with EXO70H4, and reciprocal IPs confirm the RPG-EXO70H4 interaction, though the majority of VPY does not co-precipitate with RPG under the tested conditions.
results.evaluation: The co-localization is demonstrated using FLIM to distinguish fluorophores and quantified (C44-C45, Figure 3D-F). Co-IP experiments show interactions in both directions for RPG-EXO70H4 (C46-C47), providing strong biochemical evidence. The inability to pull down VPY efficiently (C48-C49) is appropriately interpreted as suggesting most VPY is not stably associated with RPG, rather than absence of interaction. The integration of localization and biochemical data supports the infectosome model (C54, C91).

results.result: VPY recruitment to puncta is RPG-dependent: VPY-positive puncta are systematically present in WT infected (18/19) and uninfected (6/8) root hairs but absent in rpg-1 (0/19 infected, 0/8 uninfected). Ectopic co-expression of RPG with VPY in uninoculated WT roots is sufficient to recruit VPY to puncta (43/52 root hairs), demonstrating RPG is both necessary and sufficient for VPY recruitment in a symbiont-independent manner.
results.evaluation: The necessity of RPG for VPY recruitment is demonstrated by systematic quantification in WT versus rpg-1 (C50-C51) with clear frequencies showing complete loss of puncta in the mutant (C52). The sufficiency is established by ectopic expression experiments showing RPG alone can recruit VPY without symbiont (C53), with quantified frequencies (43/52). The combination of loss-of-function and gain-of-function approaches provides strong genetic evidence for RPG's role in VPY recruitment (C55, C92).

results.result: In WT roots, PI(4,5)P2 enriches at the apical membrane of uninfected root hairs and becomes locally enriched at the membrane surrounding bacteria emerging from the infection chamber and at the IT tip during active growth. PI(4,5)P2 also accumulates on the basal membrane of infected root hair cells and apical membrane of underlying cortical cells, suggesting membrane polarization occurs along the trajectory of IT propagation.
results.evaluation: The PI(4,5)P2 distribution is characterized using FLIM with the mCitrine-2xPHPLC biosensor at multiple infection stages (C58-C63). The mutant biosensor control (Figure 5—figure supplement 4) validates specificity. Phasor analysis provides quantitative validation of membrane enrichment (Figure 5—figure supplement 3). The spatial correlation of PI(4,5)P2 enrichment with infection sites is well-documented. However, C64 about the function of this polarization is speculative.

results.result: In rpg-1, PI(4,5)P2 enrichment is normal at uninfected root hair tips and at initial bacterial accommodation from the infection chamber, but fails to strongly enrich on the majority of IT membranes (21/33 ITs). Phasor analysis confirms statistically significant differences in IT membrane fluorescence between WT and rpg-1. Pre-infection responses (basal/apical membrane polarization) occur normally in rpg-1, indicating RPG is required specifically for maintaining IT-confined PI(4,5)P2 polarization, not for establishing initial polarization.
results.evaluation: The stage-specific analysis of PI(4,5)P2 distribution in rpg-1 (C65-C68) demonstrates RPG is not required for initial polarization (C67) but is essential for maintenance (C69-C70). Quantification shows 21/33 ITs lack strong enrichment (C68), and Phasor analysis provides statistical validation (C74). The observation that pre-infection responses are intact (C71-C72) supports the specificity of RPG's role in IT maintenance. The inference about synchronization (C73) is reasonable but less directly supported.

results.result: Co-visualization of PI(4,5)P2 and PI4P biosensors reveals differential membrane enrichment in WT, with PI(4,5)P2 enriched at IT tips and PI4P at the plasma membrane. This differential enrichment is reduced in rpg-1, where PI4P is similarly enriched on both membranes while PI(4,5)P2 accumulation is low at IT tips. Quantitative analysis of IT tip versus plasma membrane fluorescence ratios statistically validates these differences.
results.evaluation: The dual biosensor approach (C75-C76) provides direct comparison of two phosphoinositides, strengthening the conclusion about membrane identity. Quantitative analysis of fluorescence ratios (C77) with statistical validation supports the differential enrichment. The use of non-fluorescent bacteria (S. meliloti-LacZ) to avoid interference is methodologically sound. The data support RPG's role in maintaining localized membrane polarization (C78).

results.result: In WT, endoplasmic microtubules (EMTs) connect the nucleus to the IT tip in most infected root hairs (11/14), forming a cone-shaped array. In rpg-1, this connection is loosened or absent in the majority of cases (31/48), with EMTs appearing dispersed and IT tips frequently misoriented (19/48). The tip-to-nucleus distance is significantly increased and more variable in rpg-1 (median 63.68 μm) versus WT (median 32.16 μm), though some rpg-1 root hairs maintain WT-like connectivity, indicating RPG is required for maintaining but not establishing the tip-to-nucleus connection.
results.evaluation: The microtubule analysis uses an endogenous tubulin isoform (SYMTUB) to minimize perturbation (C79), which is methodologically appropriate. Quantification of connectivity (C80, C84) and tip orientation (C82) provides objective measures. The statistical analysis of tip-to-nucleus distance (C84) demonstrates significant differences. The observation that some rpg-1 cells maintain connectivity (C85) supports the interpretation that RPG is required for maintenance rather than establishment (C86). The inferences about loss of guidance (C81, C83) are well-supported by the data.

results.result: NPL (NODULE PECTATE LYASE) shows preferential accumulation at the IT tip in WT root hairs, consistent with prior reports. In rpg-1, NPL accumulates throughout the enlarged IT lumen without focal accumulation, indicating RPG is required to restrict NPL secretion to the IT tip.
results.evaluation: The NPL localization is assessed using live-cell imaging of NPL-GFP (C87-C88). The WT pattern is consistent with prior work (C87, citing Liu et al., 2019a), providing validation. The loss of focal accumulation in rpg-1 (C88) is clearly documented. The inference that RPG restricts the secretion domain (C89) is reasonable given the localized versus diffuse patterns, though direct measurement of secretion rates is not provided.

results.result: RPG functions as a crucial modulator of the infectosome machinery sustaining IT polar growth. The cooperative function of RPG with the infectosome complex is consistent with similar phenotypes in rpg, vpy, and lin mutants. The IT enlargement in rpg mutants reflects loss of VPY punctate localization and results in loss of PI(4,5)P2 polarization and unconfined NPL secretion.
results.evaluation: This integrative result synthesizes multiple lines of evidence: genetic (C93), localization (C94), and cellular phenotypes (C113). The consistency of phenotypes across rpg, vpy, and lin mutants (C93) supports a common pathway. The correlation between VPY mislocalization and IT enlargement (C94) is logical. The summary appropriately integrates the major findings about membrane polarization and secretion (C113). This represents a well-supported synthesis of the experimental results.

results.result: The authors propose that RPG provides specificity to a conserved cellular machinery enabling rhizobial accommodation, potentially serving as an organizational hub for infectosome assembly analogous to the polarisome in fungi. RPG may restrict exocytotic vesicle tethering to enable rapid tip growth, with loss of function causing unrestricted secretion that feeds back negatively on membrane polarization and cytoskeleton organization. IT polarity is proposed to rely predominantly on conserved mechanisms with few specific factors like RPG.
results.evaluation: These claims represent mechanistic models and hypotheses rather than directly demonstrated results. While the models are consistent with the data (C57, C99, C131), many specific mechanistic proposals are speculative: the polarisome analogy (C112), the feedback model (C126-C127), effects on actin (C128), and the vesicle tethering model (C125). The temporal confinement model (C137-C138) is reasonable but not directly tested. These represent valuable hypotheses for future work but are not experimentally validated in this study.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes RPG within broader symbiosis biology, noting that VPY and LIN are conserved in AM symbiosis while RPG is lost in non-nodulating species. The authors discuss potential connections to conserved cellular processes including PI(4,5)P2 metabolism, ROP GTPases, and actin dynamics, and draw parallels to the fungal polarisome.
results.evaluation: These claims appropriately cite prior literature to contextualize the findings (C95-C97, C100-C106, C108-C111, C114-C123, C129-C130). The citations appear accurate and relevant. The discussion of PIP5K gene expression during infection (C118) provides supporting evidence for the PI(4,5)P2 findings. However, many of these claims are primarily literature-based context rather than new results from this study. The speculative elements (C120) are appropriately qualified.

results.result: Live-cell imaging over 4-8 dpi shows WT forms thin, elongated ITs while rpg-1 infection structures appear retarded with highly variable, irregular shapes. Continuous bacterial multiplication likely leads to slow, unguided progression, supported by EMT disintegration and increased tip-to-nucleus distance. Although basal membrane polarization and PIT formation are unaltered in rpg-1, effective nodule infection is impaired.
results.evaluation: The temporal analysis of IT development (C133) is based on systematic imaging across multiple figures. The inference about bacterial multiplication driving slow progression (C134) is reasonable given the enlarged structures and is consistent with prior suggestions (citing Arrighi et al., 2008). The correlation with cytoskeletal defects (C135) integrates multiple observations. The observation about intact pre-infection responses but impaired nodule infection (C136) is directly supported by the data.
